6fd74311.title: 1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond #Shorts
6fd74311.summary: The dolphin Short most likely broke out because YouTube's Shorts feed tested it with a wider French-speaking audience and people kept watching. The likely reason they kept watching is the opening line: it says a wild animal has a human trait, a first name, and answers to it, which raises a question viewers want answered. The crow tool-making Short broke out the next day with the same 'an animal does a human thing' idea, so this looks like a repeatable topic rather than luck. The octopus and tardigrade Shorts, which were about body facts rather than minds, stayed at the usual level.
6fd74311.report:
## The numbers

- **How far above usual:** 966 views against a usual 9, about 107 times the norm.
- **Not a one-off:** the next day, '1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie' reached 1,215 views. That makes 2 breakouts out of 6 Shorts in 48 hours.
- **The ones that stayed normal:** octopus (9 views), tardigrades (12), chimpanzee Ayumu (4) and elephant (0).
- **Likes per 100 views:** dolphin 5.2 and crow 4.1. The four normal Shorts together have 5 likes on 25 views, about 20 per 100. That high rate on a tiny base is what you see when only subscribers or friends watch. A stranger audience liking at 4-5 per 100 is a healthy rate.
- **Comments:** 0 on the dolphin and 1 on the crow, even though the script planned a pinned question. **Guess:** the pinned comment was never posted, or the question ('what would your whistle sound like?') was too abstract to answer.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics returned no retention, traffic sources or countries. So I can't confirm the share of Shorts-feed traffic, the swipe-away rate or which countries watched. The Ayumu and elephant Shorts may have been only hours old when the data was pulled, so their low counts don't prove anything yet. My web search hit its limit, so I could not check news or trends for 26 October. The timing points below are reasoning, not confirmed facts.

## Hook and first 2 seconds

The opening is 'Ce dauphin a un prénom. Et il répond quand on l'appelle.' It works for three reasons:
- It is short: two sentences of plain words.
- It says something surprising as plain fact, not as a question.
- It comes with a dolphin leaping from the water and the on-screen text « Ce dauphin a un PRÉNOM. »

The viewer knows the promise in under 2 seconds. Compare the hooks that stayed flat: 'three hearts' and 'tardigrades survived UV' are anatomy facts, interesting but with no 'that's like me' moment. The crow hook (an animal bends a wire into a tool) uses the same mechanism as the dolphin one.

## Psychology

- **Seeing ourselves in the animal (watch):** a first name is one of the most human things there is. Giving it to a wild animal creates instant surprise and doubt ('really?').
- **Curiosity gap (finish):** the 'how do they know?' question only pays off at about 0:24-0:34, when the synthetic copy without the dolphin's voice reveals that the name is in the melody. **Guess:** this halfway reveal kept people watching to the end.
- **Emotion near the end (like):** the 20-year memory of old companions adds warmth and a sense of loyalty, which is a typical reason people like a video.
- **Share:** **guess** — parents sending it to children, or friends sending a 'did you know' fact, helped by the family audience during the autumn school holidays.
- **Comment:** the closing question ('would you recognise a friend's voice after 20 years?') is personal but low-energy. Nobody answered it.

## Topic and timing

The topic is animal intelligence, and specifically animals that have names. The same idea already came back in widely covered studies: elephants (2024), marmosets (2024) and dolphins (2013). It is an evergreen hit, and the science is solid (King & Janik, PNAS 2013).

Timing: it went out on Monday 26 October at 13:29 Paris time (17:59 IST) and 08:29 in Quebec. **Guess:** French Toussaint holidays (about 17 Oct–2 Nov) and Belgian autumn holidays were probably on, meaning more family viewing in the daytime. But the octopus Short went out 1h45 earlier on the same day and stayed flat, so the time slot was not the cause. I can't tell when it took off or which countries watched without analytics. I found no news peak linked to dolphins (search unavailable).

## Title, description and thumbnail

- **Title:** '1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond' follows a clear equation format: a simple unit = a human trait, then the animal doing an action in the present tense. The crow title has the same structure ('1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie').
- **Failed titles also used numbers**, so numbers are not what made the difference. The difference: the breakout titles name a **human-like ability**, while '0,2 seconde, 5 chiffres' sounds like data, not an action.
- **Description:** dense, with sources and a clear note that the images illustrate rather than show the real experiment. That builds trust, but probably did not drive views.
- **Thumbnail:** barely matters in the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm

**Guess, based on how breakouts usually look on a channel with almost no subscribers:** nearly all views came from the Shorts feed. It probably went in waves: a small test group kept watching or looped, so YouTube widened the test, and growth then stopped near 1,000. Search and external links are unlikely at this volume. Check this in YouTube Studio (Reach > Traffic sources) as soon as the data is available.

## What did not matter

- Starting the title with a number: all six titles do it.
- The time of day (same day and same slot as a flop).
- The voice, the stock footage and the watermark, which are the same on every Short.
- The sources in the description.
- The comment question (0 replies).

## Repeat this

1. Topic: an animal shows a human ability (name, tool, memory, mourning, counting), backed by a well-known experiment.
2. Hook: one surprising statement in under 2 seconds, with the animal on screen and the key word in capitals.
3. A halfway reveal that explains how scientists proved it.
4. Title: '1 [thing] = 1 [human trait] : ce [animal] [verb]'.

## Test next

- Elephant names (already published): compare it with the dolphin at 48 hours to see whether the 'names' idea works again.
- Parrots naming their chicks, crows recognising faces, mourning in orcas.
- A comment question with two easy options ('yes / no', 'dolphin or crow?') against an open question.
- A 35-40 s version against the 55 s version, to measure completion rates.

changes.rule: Make at least half of all new Short topics animals showing one human-like mental ability (names, tool making, face recognition, long memory, mourning, counting), each based on one well-known peer-reviewed experiment you can name.
Make the first line a statement of 8 words or fewer that gives a specific animal a human trait, said as a fact ('Ce dauphin a un prénom.'), with no number, date or scientist's name before second 3.
Place the 'how did they prove it' twist between 40% and 60% of the script, and end with a yes/no or two-choice question the viewer can answer in one word.
Open on the animal in motion, framed close, from frame 1, with the hook word in capitals on screen; show the experiment's reveal (copy, tool, test) as a single clear visual at the halfway point.
Write titles in the form '1 [thing] = 1 [human trait] : ce/le [animal] [action verb] #Shorts', always naming the human trait in plain words, never two figures or a measurement.
Tag every Short as 'mind' (animal mental ability) or 'body' (anatomy/survival), and after 48 hours compare views and likes per 100 views for the two groups before choosing the next week's topic mix.

35417b59.title: 1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie #Shorts
35417b59.summary: The crow Short broke out because it promises one clear, visible transformation (a straight wire becomes a hook) and shows it in the first 4 seconds, about one of the internet's best-loved 'smart animal' species. Its sister breakout, the dolphin Short, used the same '1 X, 1 Y: this animal does a human thing' pattern. That suggests the Shorts feed is rewarding this format, not the topic area or the publish hour. Retention, traffic and country data are still empty, so how it was distributed is a well-supported guess.
35417b59.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 1,215 against a usual 9, about **135×**. Only one other Short got near it: the dolphin Short (966 views, published the day before). The other four got 0–12 views.
- **Likes:** 50, so **4.1 per 100 views**. The dolphin Short had 5.2. The four non-breakouts together had 5 likes on 25 views (20 per 100). That rate is inflated by tiny samples, probably the team and early followers, so it isn't a fair comparison. 4% is a healthy rate for Shorts-feed traffic.
- **Comments:** 1, so 0.08 per 100 views. The 'compréhension ou habitude ?' prompt barely worked.
- **A detail to watch:** both breakouts stopped at exactly 50 likes. That may be a coincidence. Check it isn't a display or caching artefact.
- **What we can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics totals, traffic and countries are empty. We don't know average view duration, % viewed, swipe-away rate, whether the views came from France or abroad, or how many came from the Shorts feed versus search. Everything below about distribution is inference.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is « Un seul fil de fer, bien droit. Ce corbeau le tord… et en fait un crochet. » It shows the whole story in one visual change: straight wire, then a hook. The on-screen text « 1 fil droit → 1 crochet » repeats the title word for word, so the promise in the feed matches the payoff on screen. It uses the present tense and the pointer word 'ce corbeau', which feels like watching it happen live, not hearing a lecture. The non-breakouts opened on abstract facts: three hearts, UV in orbit, 0.2 seconds. None of those can be seen in one image.

## Psychology
- **Watch:** surprise that an animal does something people thought only humans do (making a tool, not just using one). This is the same 'animal like us' pull that made the dolphin 'prénom' Short work.
- **Finish:** a curiosity gap opens at 0:36 (as smart as a 5–7-year-old?) and gets a twist at 0:44 (the results changed). That twist is a good reason to stay to the end. This is a guess until we have retention data.
- **Like:** quiet admiration plus 'learned something solid'.
- **Comment:** weak. A one-word answer to an academic question gives viewers no personal stake.
- **Share:** probably low. With no data, assume most reach came from the algorithm, not from sharing.

## Topic and timing
The crow that solves problems is a lasting viral genre. TikTok has whole discovery pages for 'smart crow videos', and clips such as a crow sledding on a roof lid (BoingBoing, June 2026) and a crow building a perch to drink (Upworthy) went viral this year. Futura-Sciences published a French piece on crow intelligence about two weeks before. A new German study saying crows make some visual decisions about twice as fast as humans was in the news around the same days. Whether that boosted us is a guess. Halloween week may also slightly favour crow imagery (guess).

Published 15:03 IST = **10:33 Paris** on a Tuesday. The script asked for 15 h or 21 h Paris. It looks like the time was entered as IST. When it took off and which countries watched are unknown until analytics fill in.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title « 1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie » has the same shape as the dolphin winner « 1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond »: two '1's, a concrete object, then the animal plus a present-tense action verb.

The losers break that shape:
- 'pourquoi' sounds like an explainer (octopus)
- a past-tense news report (tardigrades)
- a proper name nobody knows (Ayumu)

The description is careful and well sourced, but on the Shorts feed few viewers read it. It builds trust; it doesn't create reach. The planned thumbnail matters little on the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm
A guess: with 9 usual views and no outside push, 1,215 views almost certainly came from the **Shorts feed** testing it on new viewers and seeing enough watch time and likes to widen it. Search for 'corbeau' is possible but small. Suggested and external traffic are likely close to zero. Confirm in Analytics → Traffic source.

## What did not matter
- **Hashtags:** the same on every Short, losers included.
- **Sources and AI labels:** the same on every Short.
- **Narrator voice and music:** the same.
- **The subscribe call to action:** the same.
- **Publish hour:** the octopus Short at 11:46 Paris died, and the crow at 10:33 broke out. That weakly suggests the hour didn't matter.
- **The comment question:** 1 comment.
- **Two posts on one day:** the chimp Short, 4 hours after the crow, got 4 views. It probably didn't hurt the crow.

## Repeat this
- An animal doing one **human-like act you can see**, shown in full within 4 s.
- The title shape '1 X, 1 Y : ce/le [animal] qui [verbe au présent]'.
- On-screen text identical to the title's equation.
- Famous 'smart' species: corvids, dolphins, parrots, great apes, elephants.
- A twist near the end that makes viewers doubt what they just learned.

## Test next
- Does the elephant Short (same shape, ending in '?') perform like the dolphin? Its 0 views so far are too early to judge.
- Replace the academic one-word question with a personal one, e.g. 'Votre chien ferait-il ça ?'.
- End on the opening image (the hook) so the Short loops.
- Publish at real 15 h Paris to compare with the 10:33 slot.

changes.rule: Pick topics where a well-known 'smart' animal (crow, raven, parrot, dolphin, great ape, elephant) does one human-like act that can be shown in a single before/after image, such as making a tool, answering to a name or counting. Skip topics that are only a body fact or a lab statistic.

Make the first sentence deliver the whole act in under 4 seconds: one object, one action, one result, in the present tense with 'ce [animal]'. Example: 'Un seul fil droit. Ce corbeau le tord… et en fait un crochet.'

Replace the abstract closing question with a personal, easy one that refers to the viewer's own life or pet (e.g. 'Votre chien ferait-il ça ? Oui ou non'). Make the very last line point back to the opening image so the Short loops.

Open the first 2 seconds on the before→after change itself (e.g. straight wire, then hook), with on-screen text '1 X → 1 Y' matching the title word for word. Never open on a title card, a map or a scientist.
Write titles in the form '1 [objet], 1 [résultat] : ce/le [animal] qui [verbe au présent] #Shorts'. Never use 'pourquoi', the past tense or an unknown proper name (like Ayumu) in the title.

Tag every Short as 'equation format' or 'other'. Each day, compare views and likes per 100 views for the two groups, and the elephant Short against the dolphin and crow winners, once YouTube Analytics retention and traffic data arrive.
Keep it narrator-only for animal-intelligence Shorts. Give the animal its real name (like Betty) only in the second sentence, after the hook has shown what it did.

e7a70ed3.title: 3 करोड़ वोटर कटे? याचिकाकर्ता का दावा, SC का नोटिस #Shorts
e7a70ed3.summary: This Short got about 10 times the channel's usual views (78 against 8) because it was posted the same night the Supreme Court issued notice on Maharashtra's voter-list revision (SIR). It was also the only recent Short where the viewer had something personal at stake: the question of whether their own name had been cut from the voter list. The English version of the same story beat the channel's other English Short too (20 views against 0), so the topic drove the breakout, not the language or the presentation. These counts are very small, though, and there is no analytics data yet, so treat this as an early signal rather than proof.
e7a70ed3.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 78 against a usual 8, about 9.8 times normal. The English twin of the same story, posted at the same minute, got 20. The other English Short (electoral bonds) got 0, so the English version also did far better than its comparison. The Hindi Shorts that did not break out got 7 (BRICS) and 9 (electoral bonds).
- **Comments:** 2 comments, about 2.6 per 100 views. Every other Short on the channel has 0 comments. This is the only Short so far that got people to reply.
- **Likes:** 0 per 100 views. The electoral-bonds Short got 1 like on 9 views. At these sample sizes, likes tell us nothing.
- **Retention, traffic sources, countries:** all empty in the data. We cannot yet say whether people watched to the end, whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, or whether viewers were in Maharashtra. A spike to 78 is the size of one small test batch that YouTube sends to the Shorts feed (a guess). It could also be a few search clicks on 'SIR'. What we can't know yet: average % viewed, swipe-away rate, how many views came from search, and whether the 2 comments came from real viewers or from the team.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script in the data, so this section is a guess based on the title. The opening most likely showed the number '3 करोड़' together with the question 'वोटर कटे?'. A big round number plus a question makes the viewer ask 'is that me?' in under a second. The BRICS and electoral-bonds Shorts open on events that don't touch the viewer's life today. Next time we need the script and the retention curve to confirm the hook did the work.

## Psychology
- **Personal stake and fear of loss:** the description says about one in three Maharashtra voters were cut. People respond more strongly to losing something they already have (their vote) than to news about spending or about past verdicts.
- **An open question that makes people keep watching:** the claim, the court notice, the Election Commission not yet answering, and a next hearing on 5 November. The story is unfinished, which is a reason to watch to the end and to comment.
- **Reassurance worth sharing:** the Chief Justice said no one would be prosecuted for filling Form 6, the form deleted voters are being asked to use. That is useful to forward to family (a guess on sharing; we have no share data).
- **Comment prompt:** the closing question ('क्या कोर्ट के फ़ैसले तक नाम कटना रुकना चाहिए?' – should the deletions stop until the court decides?) is a yes/no question anyone can answer. That probably explains the 2 comments.

## Topic and timing
The Supreme Court issued notice to the Election Commission, the Centre and Maharashtra on Monday 26 October without granting interim relief (LiveLaw, The Wire, Deccan Herald). The Short went up at 22:38 IST the same day, while people were still searching for the news. SIR deletions had been a national story for weeks: Rahul Gandhi's plea, the Delhi Form-6 matter and the Uttar Pradesh deletions. So the subject already had an audience, and the court notice was a fresh trigger.

**Accuracy flag:** Deccan Herald and The Federal report about **2.07 crore (21.14%)** names dropped from the draft rolls. '3 crore / one in three' is the petitioner's figure, close to The Wire's one-third estimate against 2024 electors. The description correctly says the figures are the petitioner's. The title, however, leads with the larger, contested number. To stay neutral, the official figure has to appear alongside the claim. We have no country data, but a mostly Indian audience, concentrated in Maharashtra, is a likely guess.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title has a number, a question mark, who is claiming it, and what the institution did. The question mark plus 'याचिकाकर्ता का दावा' (the petitioner's claim) keeps it neutral. It leaves out 'महाराष्ट्र' (Maharashtra) and 'SIR', the words people actually search for, although the hashtags cover SIR. The description is strong: it names its sources, gives the next date and ends on a question. The thumbnail is irrelevant on the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm
There is no traffic data. My best guess: the Shorts feed tested the video on Hindi news viewers, and comments that came in early helped it get a second batch. Search for 'SIR', 'voter list' and 'Supreme Court' on the night of the hearing may have added views. There is no sign of external sharing.

## What did not matter
- **Language alone:** both language versions did better than their comparison Shorts.
- **Publish hour:** 22:38 is late, and the BRICS Short at 01:19 still failed. Being on the same day as the news mattered, not the clock time.
- **Likes:** zero, yet the video still spread.
- **Accountability framing by itself:** the BRICS Short ('क्या ख़र्च जनता को बताया जाएगा?' – will the spending be disclosed to the public?) asked an accountability question but had no personal stake for the viewer.
- **Old verdicts:** electoral bonds is a settled story, and it did not spread.

## Repeat this
- Post the same day as a court or Election Commission action.
- Pick topics where the viewer can ask 'does this affect me?'.
- Lead with one big number, labelled as a claim.
- End on the next date and a yes/no question.
- Name every source.

## Test next
- Put 'महाराष्ट्र SIR' in the title, against the current style.
- Open with 'क्या आपका नाम कटा?' (has your name been cut?) and how to check (electoralsearch.eci.gov.in), against opening on the number.
- Post a follow-up Short on the 5 November hearing and on the final roll, to see whether a running story keeps its viewers.
- Get the retention and traffic data exported for this video and the next ones.

changes.rule: Each day, choose at least one topic that is a court, Election Commission or government action from the last 24 hours that directly affects an ordinary voter's own rights, documents or deadlines (voter list, Aadhaar, Form 6, a scheme cut-off). Rank these above summits, spending stories and past verdicts.

Open the script with one big number framed as a question the viewer can relate to (for example, 'क्या आपका नाम भी कटा?'). If that number comes from a party or petitioner, give the officially reported figure in the very next sentence, with both sources named (for example: 3 crore per the petitioner, about 2.07 crore per the draft-roll reports).

End every Short on the next official date (hearing, deadline, final list) and one neutral yes/no question viewers can answer in the comments. Where viewers have something to do, say how they can check or act (for example, 'नाम जाँचें: electoralsearch.eci.gov.in').

In the first second, put the key number and a question mark on screen in large Hindi text over a real Wikimedia photo of the institution (Supreme Court, Election Commission). Show a full-screen date card for the next hearing or deadline in the last 2 seconds.

Write titles in this pattern: '[number] [what happened]? [who claims it], [institution action]'. Include the state name and the term people search for (for example, 'महाराष्ट्र SIR') within the first 40 characters.

Have one anchor ask the viewer's personal question ('मेरा नाम कटा तो क्या करूँ?' – what do I do if my name was cut?) and the other answer only with sourced facts and the official step to take, never with an opinion.

Whenever a Short gets more than 3 times the usual views, schedule a follow-up Short on the same story's next official date (here: the 5 November SIR hearing and the final roll publication) and compare its views with the original.

650a68f1.title: चुनाव आयोग का सुप्रीम कोर्ट में जवाब: 3 SIR आदेश और Form 6 #Shorts
650a68f1.summary: The Short got 196 views against a usual 7 (28x). It came out about a day after a real news event: on Monday, 26 October, the Election Commission filed a reply in the Supreme Court defending CEC Gyanesh Kumar and its SIR decisions. The title used the same words people were already searching for (चुनाव आयोग, सुप्रीम कोर्ट, SIR, Form 6), stated the news plainly instead of asking a question, and was posted in Hindi in the early evening. Likes and comments were weak (1 like, 0 comments), so my best guess is that YouTube tested it with more viewers or it was found through search, not that viewers shared it widely.
650a68f1.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 196 against a usual 7, about 28x. The next best Short got 78 views (the Hindi '3 करोड़ वोटर कटे?' Short, 26 Oct), so this one did about 2.5x the channel's previous best.

Low likes and comments with high views usually mean the views came from people seeing it in the feed or search, not from people sharing it. **This is a guess until Studio shows the traffic sources.**

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script, so I can't check the opening line. The title already works as a hook: it names two big institutions (चुनाव आयोग, सुप्रीम कोर्ट), says something just happened ('जवाब'), and names two concrete things (3 SIR orders, Form 6). Most of the channel's other titles open with a question ('क्या…?', 'फ़ैसला किसका?'). **Guess:** if the first spoken line repeated the title's plain news ('चुनाव आयोग ने सुप्रीम कोर्ट से कहा…'), viewers had a reason to keep watching in the first 2 seconds.

## Psychology
The draw was a news gap: the Election Commission, the body under question, has now answered in court, and the court hasn't decided yet. People who have followed the SIR voter-list story since 2025 want to know what the Commission actually said. The description raised a second question (a news report counted about 14 objections by the commissioners vs. 'all three orders were unanimous'), but the comment prompt asked viewers to pick between two procedural points. That doesn't make anyone feel strongly, which fits the zero comments. Viewers watched for information, not to argue or to share.

## Topic and timing
The Statesman reported that on Monday, 26 Oct, the ECI filed a counter affidavit in the Supreme Court. It said all SIR decisions were unanimous, Form 6 was not modified, and the petition against CEC Gyanesh Kumar rests on a single news report. The Short went up at 18:18 IST on Tuesday, about a day later, while people were still searching the story. SIR is one of the few election-process topics with lasting Hindi search interest, because voters worry about their own names being cut from the rolls.

The BRICS Short (7 views, 01:19) and the English versions (20 and 0 views) also did poorly. The two Shorts posted at 02:30 and 03:06 on 28 Oct show 0 views, but they may simply be too new at the time of this export. There is no country data. **Guess:** almost all views came from India.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** a plain news headline that starts with the names people search for. It matches how Hindi news headlines covered the story, so it can show up in search and in suggestions next to those news videos.
- **Description:** the first line after 'Brands: DM us…' repeats the keywords (ECI, SIR, Form 6, फ़ाइल नोट), lists two sources and clearly says the court hasn't ruled. That helps search and keeps the channel neutral.
- **Brand line:** 'Brands: DM us' as the opening line uses up the preview text. It didn't stop this breakout, but it is the weakest part of the description.
- **Thumbnail:** not meaningful for Shorts in the feed.
- **Sources:** LiveLaw plus Organiser is a lopsided source pair for a neutral channel. Pairing LiveLaw with a wire service or a mainstream paper is safer.

## Audience and algorithm
**Guess, in order of likelihood:**
1. The Shorts feed showed it to a test batch of Hindi viewers who watch politics and court news. Because the topic was fresh, enough of them watched to earn a second batch, and then it stopped because nobody liked, commented or shared.
2. Some views came from YouTube search for 'चुनाव आयोग सुप्रीम कोर्ट' or 'SIR Form 6'.

There is no sign of external traffic. The Hindi version of the voter-cut story beat its English twin 78 to 20, which supports keeping Shorts in Hindi only, as the channel says it does.

## What did not matter
- The comment prompt (0 replies).
- Hashtags: the electoral bonds Short used the same style and got 9.
- The Wikimedia photo of the Supreme Court.
- The sample sponsor segment and the AI disclosure: neither stopped the breakout.
- Posting time on its own: a Short 54 minutes earlier the same day got 9 views.
- English versions: weaker every time.

## Repeat this
- Choose a court filing, hearing or official reply from the last 24–36 hours that names a known institution.
- Write the title as a plain statement: 'संस्था का मंच पर जवाब: संख्या + दस्तावेज़' (institution's reply at a forum: number + document).
- Use the exact Hindi words people search for.
- Say clearly in the Short that the court hasn't ruled yet.
- Post in Hindi, early evening IST.
- Follow the same story when the next step happens.

## Test next
- **Statement vs. question:** compare '3 चुनाव आयुक्त, फ़ैसला किसका?' (question, 03:06) with this Short. Then publish the next SIR follow-up with a statement-style title between 17:00 and 20:00 IST and compare.
- **Sponsor placement:** run one Short with the sponsor segment after the main point and the open question, at the very end, and see whether retention improves.
- **Comment prompt:** replace the A/B choice with a question about the viewer's own experience, e.g. 'क्या आपका नाम वोटर लिस्ट में जाँचा गया?' (Has your name been checked on the voter list?), and see whether comments rise.
- **Studio check:** after 48 hours, read the traffic sources to confirm or reject the feed-vs-search guess.

changes.rule: Pick at least one Short a day from a Supreme Court or High Court filing, hearing or official reply involving the Election Commission (SIR, voter rolls, Form 6, CEC) that was reported in the last 36 hours, and pick a new step of the SIR story whenever one is reported.

Write news titles as plain statements, not questions: start with the institution names in Hindi as people search them (e.g. 'चुनाव आयोग का सुप्रीम कोर्ट में जवाब:'), then one number and one document name, under 60 characters, ending with #Shorts.
Make the first description line the one-sentence Hindi news fact with its search keywords (e.g. चुनाव आयोग, सुप्रीम कोर्ट, SIR, Form 6), and move 'Brands: DM us…' to the last line.

Make the first spoken line, within 2 seconds, the new fact in the form 'चुनाव आयोग ने सुप्रीम कोर्ट से कहा: …', and end with one open question about the viewer's own vote or voter-list entry instead of an A/B choice.

Show the title's key Hindi words as large on-screen text over the real institution photo from the first frame, and place any sponsor segment after the main fact and the open question, never in the middle of the explanation.
Schedule Hindi political news Shorts between 17:00 and 20:00 IST instead of 01:00–03:30 IST, and publish them in Hindi only, with no English twin.

For every source pair, include at least one wire service or mainstream outlet (PTI, LiveLaw, The Hindu, Indian Express, Dainik Jagran) instead of pairing a legal site with a party-affiliated outlet such as Organiser.

cd6fd9ec.title: Il sauve une cigogne… un mâle vole 13 000 km pour elle (histoire vraie)
cd6fd9ec.summary: The stork Short got about 7.5× the channel's usual views. It was a true, named love-and-loyalty story with one big number in the title (13,000 km), and it was the only story-format Short among the channel's recent animal-intelligence facts. It wasn't a one-off: two formula Shorts (dolphin, crow) got about the same views and about the same likes per 100 views. The clearest pattern I can find is a guess: when two Shorts go up within about 2.5 hours of each other, one takes off and the other stalls.
cd6fd9ec.report:
## The numbers
- **How far above usual:** 1,300 views against a usual 172.5, about 7.5×.
- **Not unique:** it sits in a group of three. The dolphin Short has 1,185 views and the crow Short 1,232. The parrot has 620, the tardigrades 348 and the SAMPLE crow 327. Five Shorts stalled under 20 views (octopus 18, dog 9, chimp 5, elephant 4, bonobo 1).
- **Likes per 100 views:** stork 3.85. Dolphin 4.30, crow 4.06, parrot 3.39. All other Shorts together: 4.32 (162 likes on 3,749 views). So the stork Short is slightly *below* the channel on likes. What set it apart was reach, not stronger reactions.
- **Comments:** 0, against 2 comments across all the other Shorts. Nobody is commenting on this channel.
- **Retention, traffic sources and countries:** all empty in the export. That means we can't tell yet how long people watched or whether they looped it. We can't tell whether views came from the Shorts feed, search or external shares, or which countries drove it. We also don't know how long after publishing these numbers were taken, so the 4-view elephant and the 1-view bonobo may just be too new.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is « Au bord d'un étang croate, une cigogne blessée ne peut plus voler. » (By a Croatian pond, a wounded stork can no longer fly.) It works because a helpless animal gives instant stakes. But the real reward, a wild male flying 13,000 km every year, only comes at lines 10–12. For now only the title carries it. Guess: retention probably dips in the middle, during the household details (heated room, TV), and comes back when Klepetan appears. We need the retention curve to confirm.

## Psychology
- **Main emotion:** being moved (some researchers call it *kama muta*), from a rescue, loyalty and a lifelong bond. These are the most shareable feelings for families.
- **Curiosity gap:** « un mâle vole 13 000 km pour elle » (a male flies 13,000 km for her) raises an obvious question: why, and does he keep coming back? That pulls people to the end.
- **Trust:** « histoire vraie » (true story) plus named sources (AFP, CGTN) makes it worth sharing.
- **Possible drag on likes (guess):** the sad ending (Malena dies) may lower likes a little.
- **Why no comments:** the closing quote invites a quiet thought, not a reply. There is no question and no debate.

## Topic and timing
This is a famous story, reported for years by AFP, France 24, Ouest-France and CGTN, so French-speaking viewers may half-remember it. Recognition helps. Late October is when storks are wintering in Africa, which makes Klepetan's journey feel current. In France the All Saints' school holidays (vacances de la Toussaint) likely run to about 2 November, so families are home (guess, dates not checked). I found no specific news event that day; my searches were cut off.

**Publish time:** 14:36 IST = 10:06 in Paris, Brussels, Geneva, Algiers and Kinshasa; 09:06 in Dakar and Abidjan; 05:06 in Montréal. That is a good morning slot for Europe and Africa. But the chimp Short (14:41 Paris) and the dog Short (05:00 Paris) failed at similar or worse times, so the clock alone doesn't explain it. We have no country data.

**Fact check:** the timeline in the script (Klepetan returning until 2021, Malena dying in July 2021) should be checked again before any follow-up. Klepetan missed 2019 and came back in 2020.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title breaks the channel's « 1 X, 1 Y : » formula. It has a human hero (« Il sauve »), an ellipsis that delays the twist, one concrete number and the proof label « (histoire vraie) ». There is no « #Shorts » in the title. Since the dolphin and crow did as well with the formula, the title is probably not the main cause in the Shorts feed. Guess: it helps more in search and suggested videos. The description cites sources and is clear about the AI images, which is good for trust. The first frame works as the thumbnail; we have no data on it.

## Audience and algorithm
There's no traffic data. Three Shorts around 1,200–1,300 views looks like the usual Shorts-feed test pattern: a Short gets shown to a test audience, and the ones that hold attention get pushed to a larger one. Our winners pass the first test, then seem to stop around 1,300.

**The strongest pattern in the list (guess):** uploads close together seem to compete with each other.
- Octopus at 16:16, then dolphin at 17:59: dolphin won.
- Dog at 09:30, then parrot at 10:00: parrot won.
- SAMPLE crow at 18:17, then chimp at 19:11: SAMPLE won.
- Stork at 14:36, then elephant at 17:00: stork won.

In every close pair, one Short took off and the other died.

## What did not matter
- The AI-image disclosure.
- The « 1 X, 1 Y » title formula in either direction: winners and losers both used it.
- Likes per 100 views: the winner was ordinary.
- Exact clock time on its own.
- The kind of animal: birds and mammals both won and both failed.

## Repeat this
- A named, documented animal with a human or loyalty bond.
- One extreme verified number in the title and on screen.
- « (histoire vraie) » plus cited sources.
- Uploads spaced so they don't compete.

## Test next
1. Put the payoff first: open on Klepetan's 13,000 km flight, then go back to the rescue. Compare retention with this version.
2. End with a debate question (« fidélité ou instinct ? », loyalty or instinct?) and see whether comments rise above 0.
3. Try a sister story with the same shape: Dindim the penguin swimming back to João in Brazil every year. Then check whether the story format gets past about 1,300 views or stops at the same point.
4. Space uploads at least 3 hours apart and see whether fewer Shorts die under 20 views.

changes.rule: Every third Short, pick a true, source-cited story about one named animal with a human rescuer or a loyalty/return bond (e.g. Dindim the penguin and João in Brazil), not a lab-cognition fact.
In the first sentence, state the most extreme verified number together with the bond (e.g. « Chaque printemps, il volait 13 000 km pour la retrouver. »), then tell the backstory.
End every script with a one-line either/or question viewers can answer in the comments, such as « Fidélité ou simple instinct ? ».
Make the first frame a close-up of the named animal's face with the key number (e.g. « 13 000 km ») as on-screen text for the first 2 seconds.
For true-story Shorts, use the title pattern « [Human] sauve [animal]… [twist with one number] (histoire vraie) », keep #Shorts out of the title, and cite the press sources in the description.
Use the real names of the human and the animals in the narration and on screen, and keep the human hero's AI look the same from shot to shot.
Schedule each day's Shorts at least 3 hours apart, keeping the same number of uploads, and log which ones got past 1,000 views.

89ec852a.title: 1 plateau vide, 1 mot : le perroquet qui dit aucun #Shorts
89ec852a.summary: The parrot Short got 620 views, 3.6 times the channel's median of 172.5. It came 4th of 11, though, so it is a normal top-half result on a channel where Shorts either get pushed (327 to 1,300 views) or stall (under 20). The likeliest reasons are that it is a bird with a surprising, child-level mental skill, that it opens on a question and answer between a person and the animal, and that its hook is a clear paradox (an empty tray, the word « aucun ») that parents can relate to. Its likes per view were the lowest of the winning group, so wide reach in the feed carried it, not stronger engagement.
89ec852a.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 620 against the channel's usual 172.5 (that is the median of the other 10 Shorts), so about 3.6 times usual. But it ranks 4th of 11. The cigogne story (1,300), the corbeau (1,232) and the dauphin (1,185) all did about twice as well. The channel splits in two: six Shorts reached 327 to 1,300 views, and five stayed at 1 to 18. The real question is what puts a Short in the top group, not what made this one special.
- **Likes per 100 views:** 3.4 (21 likes on 620 views). The other Shorts pooled: 4.3. Each winner: cigogne 3.8, corbeau 4.1, dauphin 4.3, tardigrades 4.9, corneille 5.8. The parrot has the **lowest like rate of all the winners**, so likes did not push it. It got wide distribution and then converted to likes at an ordinary rate.
- **Comments:** 0. The whole channel has 2 comments across 11 Shorts. The planned pinned question produced nothing.
- **What we can't tell yet:** the YouTube Analytics totals, traffic sources and countries all came back empty. We have no retention curve, no viewed-vs-swiped-away share, no traffic split and no country data. The bonobo (23:30 IST) and the éléphant (17:00 IST) are hours old, so their 1 and 4 views are not a verdict yet. Web search was unavailable during this study, so news, trends and other channels' results are **not checked**.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The script opens on a question and an answer with no setup: « Combien ? » … « Six. » Then: two identical objects, « Qu'est-ce qui est différent ? », answer « Aucun ». Within 2 seconds the viewer sees a non-human answering a person's question. That is one of the strongest scroll-stoppers in animal content. The winning dauphin (« 1 sifflement = 1 prénom ») and corbeau also start with the animal doing something. **Guess:** losers like Ayumu (0.2 seconds, 5 digits) open on a statistic, not on a conversation. We should check that against their scripts.

## Psychology
- **Breaking the bird-brain stereotype (guess, but consistent):** French calls a silly person a « cervelle d'oiseau ». **All 4 bird Shorts landed in the winning group:** perroquet 620, corbeau 1,232, corneille 327, cigogne 1,300. The primates (Ayumu 5, bonobo 1) and the dog (9) did not. People expect a chimp to be clever, so the surprise is weak. A bird that grasps « nothing » breaks a belief, which opens a curiosity gap.
- **A link to children:** « souvent pas avant quatre ans » and « enfant de cinq ans » give parents a measuring stick. That suits the family audience aged 18 to 54. It is also the kind of fact people pass on (« tu savais que… »).
- **A paradox:** an empty tray and one word. Answering « nothing » is a small puzzle the brain wants to solve, which makes people keep watching. **Guess:** the halfway reveal at 0:27 helped people finish the video. Without retention data we can't confirm it.
- **Why it did not drive comments:** the closing question (« à quel âge avez-vous compris… ») asks people to remember something nobody can. Viewers had nothing easy to answer.

## Topic and timing
Alex is probably the most famous talking animal in research. **Guess:** existing recognition and older viral clips of him give the topic a head start. It went out at 10:00 IST, which is 05:30 in Paris. That is not the planned 19:00 Paris slot in the script. **Guess:** the French Toussaint school holidays (around late October to early November) put families on their phones in the morning. Not checked. Publish time does not separate winners from losers: the chienne went out 30 minutes earlier in nearly the same slot and got 9 views, while the tardigrades at 05:34 Paris got 348. No country data, so where it took off is unknown. We saw no news hook. Search failed, so we can't rule one out.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title opens with a concrete object (« 1 plateau vide »), then the animal, then a verb that sounds human (« qui dit aucun »). That 1 X, 1 Y formula is shared by winners and losers alike, so the format is not the cause. The animal and the verb are. « Le perroquet qui dit » promises speech, the strongest promise in this niche. The description is well sourced and honest (« ce n'est pas Alex »), which protects trust but is unlikely to drive reach. The « 0 ? » thumbnail is rarely shown in the Shorts feed, so it matters only in search and on the channel page.

## Audience and algorithm
There is no traffic data. **Guess:** almost all views came from the Shorts feed, because the channel is small and search for « perroquet zéro » in French is thin. The split into two groups looks like the feed's first test: a Short either passes its first small audience test or stops at about 10 views. The chienne and the parrot went out 30 minutes apart in the same format. **Guess:** they competed for the same first test audience and the parrot won.

## What did not matter
- Publish hour (same slot, opposite results).
- Hashtags (identical on every Short).
- The 1 X, 1 Y title formula (the losers use it too).
- Mixing AI images with labelled stock footage (both groups do).
- The pinned or closing question (0 comments).
- The word count of the description.

## Repeat this
- An underestimated animal, ideally a bird, doing something we think only children can do.
- An exchange between a person and the animal in the first 2 seconds.
- A clear comparison to a child's age.
- A one-word paradox in the title.
- An honest « un seul oiseau » caveat. Keep it. It costs nothing.

## Test next
- A bird versus a primate on the same skill, same day, 4 or more hours apart.
- A closing question that can be answered with one number or one word, to get comments.
- Fish, insect or reptile minds, to see whether the underestimated-animal effect goes beyond birds.
- Re-read this study once the 18:00 Paris publishing slot has comparable data.

changes.rule: Pick at least half of each day's Shorts about birds or other underestimated animals (fish, insects, reptiles) showing a skill people think only humans or young children have; use primates and dogs only when the skill truly surprises.
Open every script with a spoken question from a person and the animal's answer or action in the first 2 seconds (like « Combien ? » … « Six. »), with no context or name before it.
Include one comparison to a child's age (for example « les enfants pas avant 4 ans ») before the 35-second mark, and end with a question viewers can answer with a single number or word.
Show the animal's answer word as a large centred caption at 0:01 and repeat it as a full-screen reveal at the halfway point, in French only (never an English word on screen).

Write titles as concrete object first, then the animal, then a human-sounding verb (« le perroquet qui dit », « le corbeau qui plie »), and never reuse a recent winner's exact pattern with a different animal swapped in.

Tag every Short by animal group (bird, primate, mammal, invertebrate, other) and opening type (dialogue or statistic), and in each study compare the winning group against the stalled group on these two tags, using Shorts older than 48 hours.

7932bb04.title: क्या PM अकेले मुख्य चुनाव आयुक्त को हटा सकते हैं? #Shorts
7932bb04.summary: The Short asked a simple yes-or-no constitutional question, 'Can the PM remove the Chief Election Commissioner on his own?', hours after Rahul Gandhi said on 27 October that the SIR protests would go on until the CEC resigns or Modi removes him. That statement left many viewers with exactly this question. It was part of a run of SIR and Election Commission Shorts that all did well (302, 193 and 101 views), while BRICS, electoral bonds and English versions stayed at or below the usual 18. So the subject and the timing mattered most, and the clear question format added to it.
7932bb04.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 193 against a usual 18, about 10.7x. It is not the channel's top Short, though. 'चुनाव आयोग का सुप्रीम कोर्ट में जवाब' (27 Oct, 18:18) got 302, and '3 करोड़ वोटर कटे?' got 101. All three cover SIR and the Election Commission (ECI).
- **Likes:** 4 per 193 views, or 2.1 per 100. The other seven Shorts together got 5 likes on 464 views, or 1.1 per 100, so this one got about twice as many likes per view.
- **Comments:** 1 per 193 views, or 0.5 per 100, against 0.4 per 100 for the rest. That is about the same.
- **Hindi vs English:** the Hindi version beat its English copy every time (101 vs 29, 12 vs 0).
- **Same topic, posted soon after:** '3 चुनाव आयुक्त, फ़ैसला किसका?' went up 36 minutes later on a close topic and got 2 views.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics retention, traffic sources and countries are all empty. We can't tell whether people watched to the end, whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, or when the views came in. The script is missing, so the hook can only be judged from the title and description. With 4 likes and 1 comment, every per-view figure is noisy.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
We have no script, so this is a guess based on the title and description. The Short starts with one closed question that names a well-known office (PM) and a dramatic action (removing the CEC alone). A yes/no question creates a short curiosity gap that one answer closes: 'नहीं', then Article 324(5), then three steps. Short, finished-off answers like this tend to keep people watching to the end. The weaker Shorts start with a claim ('6 साल चली...'), an event (BRICS) or a list of documents (3 SIR orders and Form 6), which takes more effort to follow.

## Psychology
- **Curiosity gap:** on 27 October Rahul Gandhi said the agitation would go on until the CEC resigns 'or Modi removes him' (UNI). Anyone who heard that would ask whether Modi can actually do it. The Short answered that in one word.
- **Wanting a straight fact:** the subject is heated, and viewers on both sides wanted something they could check. A neutral constitutional answer can be shared by people on either side to back up their own point. This is a guess, but it fits the doubled like rate: people like a Short that settles an argument.
- **Why so few comments:** the closing question ('आपकी क्या राय है?') is vague. A sharper either/or prompt might get more comments.

## Topic and timing
- **The news cycle:** in October, SIR was the main story: Rahul Gandhi's detentions (7 Oct, Al Jazeera), the INDIA bloc march (12 Oct), the ECI affidavit to the Supreme Court saying its SIR orders were unanimous (26–27 Oct, ANI/Tribune), and talk of an opposition 'public impeachment' of the CEC.
- **Two news items asking the same question:** the ECI's affidavit said the CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge (india.com), and Rahul Gandhi's statement the same day put 'Modi removes him' into the news. Both point straight at this question.
- **Published at 02:30 IST,** a few hours after the statement, so it was ready when Indian viewers woke up. When it took off and from which countries can't be seen without Analytics. Guess: almost all India.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** short Hindi, starts with 'क्या', and names PM and CEC. It reads like something a person would type into search.
- **Description:** gives the answer in the first line ('नहीं'), then the article number, the removal process, the news hook, both sides' positions and the sources. This matches the channel's rules and gives search text to match. The 'नहीं' in the description gives away the answer, but most Shorts viewers never open the description, so it probably did not hurt.
- **Thumbnail:** Shorts get no custom thumbnail in the feed, so the first frame counts. We don't know what it was.

## Audience and algorithm
We can't see traffic sources, so this is a guess. Most views probably came from the Shorts feed, which tested the Short with Hindi political-news viewers already watching SIR content. Some may have come from search, because the title matches what people were asking ('क्या PM CEC को हटा सकते हैं'). The 302-view ECI Short the evening before may have shown YouTube that this channel's viewers respond to ECI topics. The near-zero result of the similar Short posted 36 minutes later suggests that two Shorts on one topic, posted close together, may compete for the same test viewers. That is also a guess.

## What did not matter
- **Publish hour:** results from 02:30 and 18:18 were both good, and 01:19 was poor.
- **The English versions:** they always did worse.
- **The number of sources and hashtags:** these are the same on every Short, including the weak ones.
- **Big events with no viewer question attached:** BRICS (18 views).
- **Older background stories:** electoral bonds (12 and 0 views).

## Repeat this
- Take the leader's statement of the day and pull out the legal or constitutional question it raises.
- Ask it as a closed question in Hindi: 'क्या [पद] अकेले [कार्य] कर सकते हैं?'
- Answer it within seconds, with the article number and two-sided sourcing.
- Publish within about 12 hours of the statement.
- Stay on the SIR/ECI topic while it is the main story.

## Test next
1. Put the answer in the first 2 seconds against holding it until second 5, on two 'क्या...सकते हैं?' Shorts, and compare likes per 100 views.
2. Replace the vague closing question with an either/or prompt ('क्या 324(5) की सुरक्षा सही है — हाँ या नहीं?') to test the comment rate.
3. Space two same-day Shorts on the same topic at least 3 hours apart, without cutting the number posted, and check whether the second one still gets near zero.
4. Once Analytics loads, check this Short's search share. If it is high, write more titles that match search queries.

6e66e188.title: 61 Seats: Israel Election, Netanyahu, Knesset #Shorts
6e66e188.summary: My best guess is that this Short did well because it went out on the morning of Israel's election, when a lot of people worldwide were searching for it, and it asked a question that was still unanswered: who can reach 61 seats? Its title also contained the three words people were most likely to type: Israel Election, Netanyahu and Knesset. Our other Shorts mostly had clever titles without those words, or covered stories that were already settled. The video stayed correct when the exit polls came in, so it could keep picking up views all day.
6e66e188.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 52 on YouTube against a usual 4, about 13 times normal. Plus 16 on Instagram. Only one other recent Short came close: the Alaska megatsunami Short with 33. Next were Orionid with 12 and Gaganyaan, Surrey and the Houthi claim with 10 each. The other 12 Shorts with data averaged about 3.
- **Likes:** 1 like, so about 1.9 likes per 100 views. Every other Short combined has 0 likes from about 118 views. One like is a tiny number, but it is the first time the channel has had one.
- **Comments:** 0, the same as every other Short.
- **Retention, traffic sources and countries:** YouTube Analytics returned nothing for any of these.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** whether the views came from the Shorts feed, search or a share; how long people watched; and which countries they were in. With only 52 views, one share in a group chat could explain most of the jump. Treat everything below as a likely explanation, not a proven one.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is "Sixty-one. That's the number Israel's next leader needs, and polls suggest nobody has it." It gives a number, the stakes and the unknown answer in about two seconds. The screen shows a large amber "61" over a ballot box, then a label saying "61 of 120 Knesset seats" so the number makes sense right away. But almost every Short on this channel opens with a number, and Lula ("80 Years Old") and Surrey ("10 of 10") got 3 and 10 views. So the number-first hook is our normal format, not what made this one different. What was different is that the number stood for a question still open that day.

## Psychology
- **Curiosity gap:** it asks "Coalition or another election: which comes first?" on the day people were wondering exactly that. The Lula Short, posted after the result was known, had no open question left.
- **Strong feelings:** Netanyahu divides people sharply around the world. Both supporters and critics want to know whether he survives, which pulls in viewers from both sides. (Guess.)
- **Usefulness:** the four steps (president picks, 28 days plus 14, others try, new election) give viewers something to repeat to others, which is a known reason people like and share news. That may explain the one like. (Guess.)
- **Why it kept working:** the exit polls showed no clear winner (CNN, 27 Oct), which matched what the Short said. It never went out of date that day.

## Topic and timing
It was published at 10:58 IST, which is 07:28 in Israel, about 30 minutes after voting opened. Britannica calls it one of Israel's "most contentious elections in recent history". It was the first election since 7 October 2023, and turnout was high. Polls closed at 22:00 Israel time and exit polls came out straight away, which is probably when searches peaked. Our Short was already live with the right keywords by then. Big outlets (CNN, Al Jazeera, Times of Israel) and many YouTube explainers covered the vote, which shows how much global interest there was. Countries are unknown. My guess is the US, UK, India and Israel.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title "61 Seats: Israel Election, Netanyahu, Knesset" packs in three words people actually search for. Compare "289 Protests Began at One School" (0 views) and "14 Years in Power, Lost to a List With No Leader" (3): neither names a country or a person. The description repeats "Israel", "Knesset" and "election", names its sources and includes #IsraelElection, so it probably helped search. (Guess.) The thumbnail hardly matters in the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm
With no traffic data, my guess in order of likelihood:
1. YouTube search and topic matching on election day.
2. Shorts feed tests among viewers already watching Israel-election clips.
3. A small amount of outside sharing.

The like suggests at least one viewer was genuinely engaged.

## What did not matter
- **AI hosts Arjun and Meera:** they appear in every Short.
- **Cutting every 2-3 seconds and the music level:** the same across the channel.
- **Number-first titles:** the channel uses them everywhere.
- **#Shorts and the general hashtags:** used on every Short.
- **The Instagram cross-post:** 16 views, which is normal.
- **Indian topics:** despite the Indian audience, Jio (3), Vyommitra (6), Jamia (0) and the cyclone Short (4) did poorly. The new global focus, set on 27 Oct, looks right.

## Repeat this
1. Cover big, dated global events people argue about, and publish on the day, before the result.
2. Name the country, the event and the best-known person in the title.
3. Build the Short around one question still open, so it stays correct whatever happens.
4. Include a short how-it-works sequence viewers can repeat to others.

## Test next
- **Follow-up:** post an Israel result and coalition Short within 12 hours. Does the 52-view audience come back?
- **Two Shorts for the next big election:** one on voting day and one when results come out, to see which timing wins.
- **Same topic, two titles:** one with keywords only, one with a clever angle, on similar stories.
- **Data:** look at the Analytics traffic sources once they appear, to confirm or throw out the search guess.

790fe2ee.title: 3 tardigrades ont survécu aux UV en orbite #Shorts
790fe2ee.summary: The tardigrade Short got 477 views, about 31 times the channel's usual 16, but it is not a one-off. Six of the channel's 13 recent Shorts have passed YouTube's first Shorts-feed test, and this was one of the smaller hits (the crow, dolphin and stork Shorts each got over 1,100 views). It got through because it took a famous 'indestructible' animal and opened with a fact that breaks that myth (it survived space, but the sun's UV nearly killed it), and it ended on an open question that brought in the only comment of the week.
790fe2ee.report:
## The numbers
- **477 views against a usual 15.5, about 31 times more.** But 'usual' here is a median that hides a two-camp channel. Six Shorts got 477 to 1,362 views (stork 1,362, crow wire 1,238, dolphin 1,191, parrot 762, crow 235 ms 509, tardigrade 477). Seven got 0 to 18. The tardigrade is the **smallest of the hits**, so the real question is what the hits share.
- **Likes per 100 views: 3.98** against 3.88 for the rest of the channel (198 likes on 5,109 views). That is normal for a hit here (dolphin 4.28, crow 4.04, stork 3.67, parrot 2.76).
- **Comments: 1, which is 0.21 per 100 views**, against 0.02 for the rest of the channel (1 comment on 5,109 views). That is about 10 times the rate, but it is a single comment.
- **Retention, traffic sources and countries: empty.** We can't yet tell what share watched to the end, whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, or which countries watched. The 0-view bee and 47-crows Shorts, and the 4-view bonobo, went out less than a day before this data was pulled, so they don't count as flops yet.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is « Ils ont survécu au vide de l'espace. Les UV du soleil, eux, en ont presque eu raison. » Sentence one gives the myth everyone already knows. Sentence two breaks it straight away. On screen, a macro shot of a tardigrade with « Vide ✅ UV complets ⚠️ » shows the twist before the voice has finished it. The losing Shorts mostly open on a plain fact (octopus: 3 hearts) or a name nobody knows (Ayumu), with no twist.

## Psychology
- **Watch:** a curiosity gap built on a known myth. Most people have heard that tardigrades are 'indestructible', so « presque eu raison » makes them want to know what nearly beat it.
- **Finish:** the numbers come in steps (10 days, 270 km, 3 survivors, 7,000 kJ/m²), and the big « 3 survivants » card at 0:42 pays off what the title promised. *Guess:* that card held people to the end.
- **Comment:** the ending leaves the question open (« La question reste ouverte ») and then asks for a one-word answer. A low-effort ask after an unsolved puzzle is the best-known trigger for comments. This was the only Short with that structure, and it got the comment.
- **Share/like:** a small animal beating space, plus a scientist-style 'nobody knows yet', is the kind of thing you send to someone. *Guess*, since we have no share data.

## Topic and timing
Tardigrades are one of the internet's evergreen stars, popular because they seem almost indestructible. October 2026 also had tardigrade stories in the news: the ACS press release on tardigrade proteins protecting frozen blood (8 Oct), and French regional press around 11 Oct on Montpellier researchers « percent les secrets du tardigrade ». So French readers had recently seen « survit au vide spatial » headlines. Nothing happened on 27 October itself, no news and no holiday, so the ambient interest probably helped and a same-day trigger didn't (*guess*). It was published at 10:04 IST, which is **05:34 Paris**, 04:34 Dakar/Abidjan and 00:34 Montreal. That is not the 15:00 or 21:00 Paris slot the script planned. We can't see countries yet.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title « 3 tardigrades ont survécu aux UV en orbite » has a number, a famous animal named plainly, a past-tense result and an unusual setting. Every hit except the 235 ms crow follows that pattern: « répond », « plie », « dit aucun », « vole 13 000 km ». Among the losers, Ayumu is a name viewers don't know and the title has no verb. The elephant title ends in a question mark and copies the dolphin title from the day before. The octopus title states a mild preference. *Guess:* a clear, surprising result in the title matters. The description (sources, Paris-Caen comparison) builds trust but is barely seen in the feed.

## Audience and algorithm
With no traffic data, the pattern points to the **Shorts feed**. Hits on this channel land between 500 and 1,400 views, and losers stall under 20. That looks like YouTube testing each Short on a small group of viewers and only pushing it wider if they stop scrolling and keep watching. Search may add a little, because « tardigrade » is a searched word, but it wouldn't produce this jump-or-nothing pattern. There is no sign of outside traffic.

## What did not matter
- **Publish time:** the parrot at 05:30 Paris got 762 views, and the dog at 05:00 Paris got 13.
- **Starting the title with a number:** every Short does it, hits and losers alike.
- **Hashtags, the thumbnail plan and the length (~57 s):** the same on all of them.
- **Narrator-only vs story:** both formats appear among the hits and the losers.

## Repeat this
1. A famous animal plus a twist that breaks its myth, inside the first 2 seconds, in voice and on-screen text together.
2. Numbers that build towards one big card showing the payoff.
3. End on a real open question and ask for a one-word answer.
4. Title pattern: number + common animal name + past-tense result + unusual setting.

## Test next
- A tardigrade follow-up that answers « qu'est-ce qui les protège ? » (Dsup and other protective proteins, the October 2026 blood-freezing study), to see whether the open-question ending builds a series.
- A question-mark title against a statement title on the same type of topic.
- A twist hook against a plain-fact hook on two famous animals the same week.
- One more true story with a human and an animal, like the stork (1,362 views, the top Short).

Write the first two sentences as myth then twist, both inside 3 seconds (e.g. « Ils ont survécu au vide. Les UV, eux, ont failed de les tuer. » style). End every script with the question the study leaves open, followed by « Un mot en commentaire ».
Make shot 1 a close-up of the animal itself with the twist on screen as a two-part text card (✅ / ⚠️) from frame one. Put one big payoff-number card between 0:35 and 0:45.

Build every title as number + the animal's everyday French name + a past-tense result verb + an unusual setting or condition, ending in #Shorts. Never lead with a proper name viewers don't know (Ayumu, Kanzi) and never end the title with a question mark.
For every third Short, build the story around a named human-animal pair from a documented true story, like the stork rescuer. Keep the narrator-only format for study-result Shorts.

Judge each Short only after 48 hours, and log it as a hit (300 views or more) or a miss together with its hook type (twist or plain fact), how famous the animal is, and whether the title has a past-tense result verb. Re-rank these factors every 10 Shorts.

3527d1b8.title: SAMPLE | 235 ms pour décider : la corneille #Shorts
3527d1b8.summary: The crow Short didn't really break out on its own. Instinct's Shorts tend to land in one of two groups: most get under 20 views, and six of the 13 (this one included) got 477 to 1,362. It got into the larger group because it carried a precise, surprising number ('235 ms') about a corvid. It went out on 27 Oct, the day after French science sites covered the Science study on 26–27 Oct, and the like rate (4.1 per 100 views) matches the channel's other higher-view Shorts. Retention and traffic data are missing, so the exact route it took to viewers is still a guess.
3527d1b8.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 509 against a channel median of 15.5, about 33 times higher. But that median hides a two-group channel. Six of 13 Shorts got 477–1,362 views (cigogne 1,362, corbeau 1,238, dauphin 1,191, perroquet 762, **corneille 509**, tardigrades 477). The other seven got 0–18. So this Short joined a group that already exists; it didn't create a new one.
- **Likes per 100 views:** 4.1 (21/509). The other higher-view Shorts average 3.8 (191/5,030), ranging from 2.8 for the parrot to 4.3 for the dolphin. The channel as a whole is 3.9. The low-view Shorts show about 10.6, but on roughly 47 views, which probably means the owner's own circle. So this Short was liked at a normal rate, no better.
- **Comments:** 0. The whole channel has 2 comments across 5,586 views. Nothing got people talking.
- **Can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics came back empty: no retention, no swipe-away rate, no traffic sources, no countries. Whether it was pushed by the Shorts feed, search or France specifically is a **guess**. The two Shorts at 0 views were published just before this data was pulled, so they don't count yet.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
We don't have the script. The title, which probably shows as the opening caption, starts with a precise, odd number: '235 ms'. All six higher-view Shorts start with a concrete number or a short story setup. **Guess:** the opening line said the 235 ms out loud and compared it to humans ('twice as fast as you'). The French press framed the story exactly that way.

## Psychology
- **Feeling challenged by a bird:** 'a crow decides faster than you' prods the viewer's ego. It's a clean curiosity gap: how can a brain without a cortex do that?
- **A number you can repeat:** '235 milliseconds' is easy to quote to someone else, which helps sharing (guess: we have no share data).
- The description ends with 'Réflexe ou décision ?', but it got no comments. The question probably never appeared on screen or in the voice-over.

## Topic and timing
- The Science paper (Schmidbauer & Nieder) came out on 22 Oct 2026. French coverage followed on 26–27 Oct (Trust My Science, Consoglobe, Martin Cid FR), with English coverage (Earth.com, Science podcast) at the same time. The Short went out at 13:47 Paris time on 27 Oct, right during that French wave. People who had just seen the headline were primed to watch.
- **Birds are a pattern:** all four bird Shorts old enough to judge did well (cigogne, corbeau, corneille, perroquet). All five mammal or octopus Shorts did badly (chimp Ayumu 5, bonobo 4, elephant 7, dog 13, octopus 18). That's a small sample, but it's the cleanest split in the data.
- **Guess:** Halloween (31 Oct) gives crows a bit of extra seasonal pull.
- Countries: unknown. My guess is France, Belgium and Quebec, where the news ran.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- The title follows the house formula, 'Number : animal + action', which shows up among both the hits and the flops. So the formula is necessary but not enough on its own.
- The 'SAMPLE |' prefix and the paragraph about a fictional partnership didn't stop it. Most viewers in the Shorts feed never read titles or descriptions.
- The full source list (Science DOI, Tübingen) builds credibility, but it doesn't drive reach.

## Audience and algorithm
Most likely route (**guess**): the Shorts feed tested it with a seed batch of viewers. It cleared the bar and got a second batch, then stalled at around 500 views. The like rate is the same as the other higher-view Shorts, so all six were probably judged the same way, on retention. The flops probably failed in the first test. Search could have added a little, since people were searching 'corneille 235 millisecondes' that week, but that's unproven.

## What did not matter
- **Publish hour:** hits went out at 05:34, 10:33, 13:29 and 13:47 Paris time. Flops went out at 05:00, 12:30 and 14:41.
- **Hashtag:** the biggest Short (cigogne) has no #Shorts tag.
- **Sponsorship text and the SAMPLE label** made no visible difference.
- **Repeating a topic:** the dolphin 'name' Short hit, but the elephant version of the same idea flopped. Copying a format to a new animal doesn't carry the hit with it.

## Repeat this
1. Cover a peer-reviewed animal study within 3–7 days of its release, while French media are still running it.
2. Lead with one precise, surprising number plus a 'versus you' comparison.
3. Prefer birds, especially corvids and parrots, along with cetaceans and extreme survivors like tardigrades.
4. Keep the sources in the description.

## Test next
- Put a yes/no question on screen in the last second to break the zero-comment streak.
- Try the same bird-plus-news formula with and without the '(histoire vraie)' story framing that the stork Short used.
- Once Analytics is connected, compare retention at 3 s and 100% between the hits and the flops. That's what confirms or kills the retention guess above.

Make the first spoken line the study's most surprising number plus a direct comparison with the viewer, e.g. '235 millisecondes : deux fois plus vite que toi.'
End every script with a one-line either/or question to the viewer (e.g. 'Réflexe ou vraie décision ? Dis-le en commentaire') and have it shown on screen too.
Show the key number as large on-screen text over the animal from frame one, and keep the animal on screen in the first 2 seconds rather than a title card or AI-generated scene.

Never put 'SAMPLE' or internal labels in a public title. Write the title as 'number + animal + the human comparison', and add one line to the description naming the journal and month it came out (e.g. 'Étude publiée dans Science, octobre 2026').

Every week, split Shorts into those above and below 300 views and record animal group, news age in days, hook number and publish hour for each, so the bird and news-timing patterns can be confirmed or dropped.

fa96630f.title: Ep 16 | 100 दिन का रिश्ता: साठवें दिन की धमकी, रिया का सच और कबीर का साथ

fa96630f.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** Ep 16 got 50 views. The median of the other 15 Shorts is 7, so it did about 7x the usual. Ep 15, posted 11 minutes earlier, got 42. Together the two make up 92 of the channel's 217 total views (42%).
- **Likes and comments per 100 views:** Ep 16 has 0 likes and 0 comments. Ep 15 has 7.1 likes per 100 views. The rest of the channel averages 3.0 likes per 100 (5 likes on 167 views). - **Retention, traffic, countries:** YouTube Analytics came back empty for all three, so we don't know who watched, from where, or for how long.
- **What the numbers can't tell us yet:** whether views came from the Shorts feed or from people opening Ep 15 and then Ep 16 on the channel page; how much of the episode people watched; and whether 50 views is real lift or one small test batch from YouTube. Ep 16 is also the newest upload, so it has had the least time to collect views. That makes the jump more likely to be real, but not certain.

**Publish time is the clearest pattern in the data:**
- Ep 1 at 04:06 IST: 2 views.
- Ep 2–4 at midday (12:10–14:18): 20–22 views each.
- Ep 5–10, six uploads 7–8 minutes apart: 0–8 views each.
- Ep 12–14 between 00:09 and 01:43 at night: 2–12 views.
- Ep 15–16 at 07:30–07:45 on a Wednesday morning, after a 30-hour gap: 42–50 views.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is an accusation said straight to her, with a name and an object in hand: 'ये फ़ोन किसका है, रिया? झूठ मत बोलना... आज नहीं।' (Whose phone is this, Riya? Don't lie... not today.) There's no scene-setting. A viewer gets a conflict (a hidden phone), a relationship (a couple) and a stake (a lie) at once, without needing Ep 1–15. The phone buzzing a moment later adds a second jolt. Guess: this cold-open confrontation works better for new viewers than episodes that open by continuing the story.

## Psychology
- **Curiosity gap twice over:** 'कौन-सी डायरी?' (which diary?) is answered inside the episode. Then 'कल रात तुम कहाँ थे?' (where were you last night?) is left open, and the episode cuts to black on Kabir's half-lit face. That's a classic open loop that pulls people to the next episode.
- **Feeling:** first fear (he catches her lying), then relief (he says 'साथ में', together), then betrayal (now he's the suspect). The swing from relief to suspicion is what K-drama cliffhangers are built on.
- **Why no likes or comments:** the question at the end is perfect for a comment ('Kabir is hiding something'), but nobody asked for one. Ep 16 having more views than Ep 15 suggests some people watched the two back-to-back (guess).

## Topic and timing
Fake marriage with a countdown, a secret about a dead or missing mother, and a stolen diary are K-drama staples adapted for Indian homes. The title's 'साठवें दिन' (60th day) is a concrete deadline inside the 100-day contract, which gives the stakes a number. Searches found no big news or viral moment tied to this on 28 October 2026. Chhath is 13–16 November, so it doesn't explain anything. Guess, not checked: Karwa Chauth, a festival about husbands and wives, falls around the end of October 2026. That might have given a married-couple drama a small seasonal boost. With no country data we can only assume viewers were in India, judging by the publish slot and the Hindi. The jump probably happened in the morning commute window, 07:30–10:00 IST.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title packs three beats in a row: a threat, a confession, an alliance. It's specific ('साठवें दिन की धमकी', the 60th-day threat) where earlier titles were vaguer ('दादी की शर्त', grandma's condition). It still opens with 'Ep 16', which tells a stranger they've missed 15 parts (guess: this costs cold clicks). The description ends on the cliffhanger question, which is good, but doesn't ask for a comment. All episodes use the same hashtags, so hashtags didn't make the difference. We have no thumbnail data, and Shorts in the feed mostly don't show one anyway.

## Audience and algorithm
Without traffic data this part is a guess. The most likely story: YouTube gave the morning pair a fresh test batch in the Shorts feed, because nothing had been posted for 30 hours.
